utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-05-87, the Prosecutor versus Nebojsa Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May we have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm Tom Hannis on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. I'm assisted today by our case manager, Ms. Susan Grogan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. And for the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am John Ackerman, together with Aleksander Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have scheduled this hearing to deal with Mr. Pavkovic's motion for provisional release. We are particularly concerned with the first prong of the test in Rule 65, whether if released the accused will turn up for trial and in that regard we are also interested in the guarantees being offered. Mr. Ackerman, do you have witnesses to call?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're going to call a witness, the Ministry of Justice is here in the courtroom and I think you know him, I think he's testified before, and he will testify with regard to the guarantees, and I think that will be sufficient to put the matter before you appropriately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So he will be your only witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So let Mr. Stojkovic take the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The government of the Republic of Serbia has passed a decision giving guarantees for provisional release --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you're going to give evidence, I think it's better that you give it from the normal place and make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. Ackerman, you lead the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what I was going to ask you, Your Honour, if you prefer it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell the Judges your name, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I am Minister of justice in the government of the Republic of Serbia. My name is Zoran Stojkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you asked to come here today to testify regarding the guarantees issued by your government for the accused Nebojsa Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The government has accepted that obligation and has passed a decision designating me as the person who will elaborate on the government's guarantees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you to do that now. I'd like you to tell the Chamber the nature of those guarantees and the -- the conditions of those guarantees and what the government will do to make sure they're properly enforced.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with the law on cooperation with the Tribunal, the government has issued guarantees in case of all persons who voluntarily surrender to The Hague Tribunal. The guarantees are very clear. We accept to issue guarantees. If General Pavkovic is released, we take it upon ourselves to ensure his presence here at the Tribunal whenever the Tribunal so requires. What is most important is that we accept all conditions specified by the Tribunal, conditions for provisional release of General Pavkovic. All of the conditions set by the Tribunal should be -- shall be complied with by us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have just two important questions that I do want to ask you. Based upon your knowledge of General Pavkovic, do you have any reason whatsoever to believe that he would not appear for trial when ordered to do so by this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In conversations with General Pavkovic, it was agreed that he would appear, or rather, surrender to this Tribunal voluntarily. And I do not think that in case that he is provisionally released he would fail to appear here voluntarily. In case he does fail to appear here voluntarily, our government will ensure his presence before the Tribunal. Therefore, I do not expect any problems in that regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your government prepared to enforce and carry out any conditions regarding his release that might be ordered by this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: We have several similar cases where persons were provisionally released and are living at liberty until their call to come back. We have complied with all of the conditions set by the Tribunal and are regularly informing and reporting back to the Tribunal. In the seven cases that we have had so far, there have been no problems in terms of compliance with the conditions. There are also possibilities to check the apartment or visit the apartment of the accused without prior notice, to contact them, to ensure that they receive prior consent before they go on any trips in accordance with the conditions set by the Tribunal. And so far, I don't think that we have failed to fulfil any of our obligations in the previous seven cases. In one of such cases after two years of provisional release and two years of staying in the country, one of the accused voluntarily returned back to The Hague when called to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you're telling us is your government would be perfectly willing to go along with any conditions that this Chamber might set for General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's right. All of that is stated in the government's decision, and as I've stated earlier in previous cases we have complied with all of the conditions and obligations, and we have received no criticism so far.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based upon your knowledge, do you have any reason to believe that General Pavkovic would be any kind of a -- of a threat or a danger to any witness that might appear before this Tribunal or in any other respect at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that there is any danger of that. According to the information I have, General Pavkovic has already cooperated with the Tribunal. During the time that he was at liberty, there have been no problems or no issues arising with the victims or witnesses or any other participants in the proceedings. So far, we have had no such problems. And as I've said, he has spent quite a lot of time at liberty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned to the Chamber that you had -- you had talked with General Pavkovic at the time he was going through the process of surrendering voluntarily to the Tribunal. Is there any question in your mind about whether his surrender to the jurisdiction of this Tribunal was voluntary or not? Was that a voluntary surrender, from your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I have to specify that I did not speak with Mr. Pavkovic personally. I think that he was ill at the time. We had contacts through his counsel. And at the time, the conditions set was to ensure proper medical examination. I think that there was a serious medical issue or a surgery. In that case, we accepted the conditions set at the time. And as far as I know, there were no other contacts or conversations based on which I could conclude that he did not wish to surrender. No coercion existed in the case. He came here voluntarily after he completed his medical examination at the military medical academy. Following that, he came to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say to your knowledge that that period of time between the time he may have become aware of an indictment by this Tribunal and his actual surrender was a time that he was undergoing medical treatment. Was that what you were advised?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: He was undergoing a treatment. To be quite clear, had we had any -- any notion that this was not a voluntary surrender we would not have given any guarantees, because voluntary surrender is a precondition for giving any guarantees. In the previous period, there was an issue -- there was a problem because for a while it was believed that he ought to stand trial in our country and it was also believed that it would be dangerous to transfer him to the Tribunal. That was before our time. When our government came to power, all of that was set aside and the new proceedings were initiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm interested in the evidence the minister said where voluntary surrender is precondition for giving any guarantees. Do you have any provisions in the rules or statute? If you could elaborate on that matter, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I think this is regulated by Article 46, but don't quote me on this; I would have to verify it. This is referred to in the conclusion, in the text of the conclusion. Article 36 of the law on cooperation with the international tribunal, which regulates the cases where the person surrenders voluntarily, it is further specified that in those cases the government will issue guarantees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And on the issue of guarantees, if they are satisfied that the surrender is voluntary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if the accused surrenders voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that at all, of that provision. Because otherwise without that condition the government would not be able to issue guarantees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkovic, you said that the circumstances in which Mr. Pavkovic would be tried remained in doubt until your government came to power. When was the date of that change of power?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it was sometime in March of 2004. Following that for a while we were awaiting for the new council for cooperation for the Tribunal to be set, and after that there was a conclusion reached that certain persons ought not to be extradited for fear it would endanger the national security. But after that the position was changed and some 15 people surrendered voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take it by that answer that by March of 2004, both you as the government and Mr. Pavkovic as the accused were aware of the existence of this indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but the government -- the current government was elected in March of 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, did I not say that? So can I take it that by March 2004 you, as a government, and Mr. Pavkovic, as the accused, were both aware of the existence of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. However, we inherited a conclusion reached by the previous government. In addition to that, we need six or seven months to organise new agencies at the level of Serbia and Montenegro and also to set up the new council for cooperation because that was the body entitled to contact the Tribunal. And following that, we set aside the conclusion reached by the previous government and then proceeded to comply with our obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what was the conclusion reached by the previous government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army passed a decision concerning Generals Pavkovic and Lazarevic, stating that their extradition could endanger the national security. And a similar one was reached concerning General Lukic by the following government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that decision formally announced so that it was common public knowledge? Or was it a state secret?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, concerning the decision passed by the previous government it was published. And as for the other one, I really couldn't tell you. I'm not sure of it. I had occasion to see the opinion issued by the General Staff. Because this had to do with two members of the army and a member of police. So in each of these cases, the responsible agency was different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Minister, when did the issue of his ill health arise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we passed the decision to set aside the decision of the previous government, we started analysing the documentation and started negotiations. We received certain documentation, and once the negotiations started we accepted the conditions and the obligation to organise proper medical examination at the military medical academy. I believe that all pertinent documentation was forwarded to the Tribunal. I think that this had to do with a surgery to receive [as interpreted] a cancerous growth in one of the organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Hannis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Minister, you mentioned at page 3, line 21, you mentioned that there were discussions with Pavkovic. You've told us since that you were not personally involved in those discussions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I've said so in order to avoid any miscommunication. I spoke to the counsel, to Defence counsel of Mr. Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of the Defence counsel that you spoke with?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that it is this gentleman sitting here, but somebody taller and slimmer. I think his name is Mr. Visnjic, but I can verify that. I know that he came to our office and brought with him medical documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- that you fit that description.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a member of the military who worked for the Prosecution and then switched and opened a private practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I can clarify that for Your Honours if you'd like me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, who was the counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ljubisa Zivadinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, Ljubisa Zivadinovic. I know that this is how he described himself to me, that he was a former military prosecutor who opened up a private attorney practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said discussions were had with Pavkovic in which it was agreed that he would appear, or rather would surrender voluntarily. How many discussions were had? How many times did you speak with his attorney?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think three or four, not with him but rather with the attorney.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct. Do you recall the first time you had a discussion with his attorney, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Probably three to four months prior to surrender. That was when the first contact took place, when we received medical documentation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I tell you he appeared here in The Hague on about I think April 25th of this year, are you saying that first discussion was three or four months prior to the 25th of April, 2005?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Perhaps it was in February or March. This is as precise as I can be, but don't hold me to it because I'm not very good with dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the last time you were here and testified in relation to a release hearing for the accused Milutinovic, Ojdanic, and Sainovic? Do you recall that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall me at that time asking you some questions about your knowledge of where Mr. Pavkovic was, because he was still a fugitive at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any information indicating that he was a fugitive. I'm telling you now that I did not see him after he went to The Hague. All I'm saying is how it transpired, what kind of contacts took place, and what kind of conditions was set for the government, namely that medical examination take place and that his family be allowed to visit him in The Hague. That's as far as I was involved. This was discussed in the contacts that I had. I think that it was Mr. Loncar, my colleague, who escorted General Pavkovic to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Minister, when you were here previously and we were addressing the matter of guarantees for those other accused, I asked you about what efforts your government had taken to arrest Mr. Pavkovic for whom a warrant had been issued sometime previously. And you indicated that you were not aware of where he was. You've just testified that you were speaking with his attorney in February or March of this year.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I have told you, the attorney brought the documents indicating that Mr. Pavkovic was ill, that he needed treatment, asking that he be allowed to undergo an examination and so on. But at the time, I did not know where Pavkovic was because I had no contact with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those medical documents reflect the name of a doctor or a clinic or a hospital at which that information had been obtained?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Some documents pertain to a type of surgery, and the other documents had to do with a gland. That's as far as I can remember. There are two types of documents. I still have them in my office and I can check and get back to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone else involved in these discussions between you and Mr. Zivadinovic, pardon my pronunciation, anyone else other than you and General Pavkovic's attorney? Just the two of you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zivadinovic would come to the ministry and he and I would have conversations, just the two of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any record made of those discussions? Notes taken, a transcript made, a tape-recording made?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any documents created as a result of the agreement that was reached between you and Mr. Zivadinovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. The agreement was as I have described to you. We ensured that General Pavkovic is allowed to go to the military medical academy to be examined, and following that he went to The Hague escorted by Minister Loncar. I was not involved in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ackerman phrased his questions to you in terms of your knowledge of the accused Mr. Pavkovic. What exactly is the basis of your knowledge? Do you know him personally? Do you know the general?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever met him before?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what is the basis of your knowledge of him? Is it based on public statements to the media, information provided to you by internal reports? What is your basis of knowledge about Mr. Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but let me be as specific as possible. I saw Mr. Pavkovic on one occasion when he was a candidate running for the president of Serbia. He came to submit his documents, and I was a member of the Republican Commission for Elections. And on that occasion we exchanged greetings; that's the extent of our contact. As for the rest, all I know is from the press.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're aware since the -- well, let me tell you this: The indictment against him was made public in late October 2003. Would you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was then. I cannot be certain of that because at the time I was not a member of the government, and I'm not aware of all the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that -- would it be fair to characterise the general as not being media shy, and as a matter of fact, he's made a number of appearances between October of 2003 and his appearance here in April of this year discussing his position about coming to The Hague. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think there is a minor misunderstanding there. All kinds of things appeared in the media, all kinds of things. The first time when I talked to Mr. Pavkovic's attorney, shortly after that I stated that I would like to talk to Mr. Pavkovic myself to verify whether it was true what was published in the media. And it turned out that a lot of that was not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how -- how do you mean "a lot of that" -- what do you mean Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. specifically "a lot of that," and how do you know it turned out it was not true? So what exactly are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Had you been able to read all kinds of articles and to see all kinds of statements given by so-called friends, you would see for yourself that there were all kinds of stories there. Therefore, after the first contacts were made when we realised that he was willing to go to The Hague voluntarily, I stated that I would like to see General Pavkovic personally to hear from him what his position was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you get that opportunity?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Because as I said in the second stage of this process I was not involved; it was my colleague who escorted General Pavkovic to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have one packet of documents that I would like to have marked as an exhibit. I want to show the witness a few of those entries and ask him some questions about that, if I could do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And while that's being handed around, let me explain what this is, Your Honours. These are -- these are entries that were taken off the web site on the Internet for a media in Serbia called B92. There are both B/C/S and English versions of stories about Mr. Pavkovic. It's apparent that the B/C/S version and the English version are not identical. It appears that the English blurb is a summary, perhaps, at best. But what I want to do is read some of the quotations that are attributed to Mr. Pavkovic and ask this witness about them. If we could show him the document. Does it have a number for purposes of this hearing? I don't know what your procedure is, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are these different from the schedule that you submitted in the opposition to the motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Some are the same, some are different, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Stojkovic, this has a -- your copy should have a page number in the bottom right-hand corner in the circle, and the first one I would like to take you to is page 46 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I didn't know he was prepared to go forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Minister, just wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I simply to state I guess in the form of an objection that it's my view that to the extent any of these articles represent statements made by General Pavkovic previously that he under no conditions would come to The Hague, that those are irrelevant to any issue that's going on here today because he did in fact come to The Hague. So obviously they were not correct and not true. He in fact did volunteer and come here. So they are no evidence that he won't come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's anticipatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think they're irrelevant for that reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's see what the article says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, many of these are statements to the fact. I have an argument about why I think they are relevant to your decision today. So I don't know if you want me to address that argument first or ask him about these and make my argument later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ask him about them and then we will hear the argument afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to go to page 46, if you have that in front of you. There are handwritten numerals in the lower right-hand corner of the pages. And for the interpreters, the top half of this page is the B/C/S version of this story dated the 9th of November, 2003, a couple of weeks after the indictment became public. The English version is titled "Pavkovic: 'I have no reason to surrender.'". And reading from the second paragraph it says: "I have no reason to surrender. I am a soldier, and our regulations state that a soldier never surrenders.' Pavkovic said late last night in an interview with Jagodina Television Palma Plus." You didn't happen to see that interview, Mr. Stojkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next if you would go to page 43, this is a report that purports to come from SRNA, S-R-N-A, on the 13th of March, 2004, and it quotes Mr. Pavkovic as saying: " 'There can be no talk of me surrendering to The Hague Tribunal. I won't even discuss it.' Pavkovic is quoted as saying in today's Glas Javnosti." Can you tell us what SRNA is, S-R-N-A?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think this is the news agency of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next if you would go to page 42, and this purports to be from Beta. Do you know what Beta is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a news agency from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is dated the 18th of April, 2004. I'm reading from the first two paragraphs in the English: "Nebojsa Pavkovic said today that he is determined not to appear before The Hague Tribunal and will not allow himself to be extradited. " 'If they extradite the three generals, and I don't include myself out because I will not allow that to happen, this government will be signing its own death warrant,' he told Podgorica Daily Publika.'" Did you see that interview or read that story at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't, and I had no opportunity to discuss that with General Pavkovic. But I must say that all of the three generals mentioned as purported by the articles claim they wouldn't come here, but they're here and they are under the competence of this Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you would go to page 39. This is from B92 dated the 21st of June, 2004. Reading from the English it says: "Pavkovic said today that he will not turn himself into The Hague where he is wanted for war crimes. "Pavkovic said that he will only appear before Serbian courts to answer any charges associated with the Tribunal. "Pavkovic said he had an 'unofficial' talk with Serbia and Montenegro Defence Minister Prvoslav Davinic." Are you aware that the general had apparently had some sort of official discussions with the defence minister?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That article goes on to say that: "Davinic said that he understood Pavkovic's reason for not wanting to turn himself in and would try to work something out in order to have him appear before a Serbian court." Do you know, apart from your discussions with General Pavkovic's lawyer, you don't know whether or not General Pavkovic and his lawyer were having discussions with other government officials or private individuals about circumstances under which he would come to appear before this Tribunal, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Let me clarify. Minister Davinic is the minister of defence of Serbia and Montenegro and not of the Republic of Serbia. So he wasn't a part of this government and I'm not familiar with those details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one more in this vein. If you could go to page 35. This also is from B92 dated the 3rd of July, 2004. The English is titled "Pavkovic makes threats." And reading from the English it says: "Nebojsa Pavkovic responded today to the news of his indictment, which arrived from The Hague yesterday by threatening members of the Serbian government. "Pavkovic said that he will have his revenge towards every person who would be potentially responsible for extraditing him and three other generals to The Hague. "No one other than me can make decision regarding my life. I can only advise them that, no matter what they decided to do, I will see my revenge." Were you aware of this threat by Mr. Pavkovic concerning any potential extradition of him to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that I am not familiar with the threat since I'm one of the members of the government who made -- who issued a document that the general would not be extradited to the Tribunal. And to speak honestly, I feel no fear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I have two others that are related to another matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I didn't understand the last answer. Do you understand it, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was whether I was familiar with the threat, and I said no, although I am a member of the government who participated in that, but we never received any threat and I do not have any sense of fear. I am here in The Hague as were the others, without protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The transcript says that you were one of the members of the government who issued a document that the general would not be extradited to the Tribunal. Is that a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We set aside the previous document. The government of which I am a member issued a decision putting aside the earlier government's conclusion that there will be no extraditions. This is what I meant, although I am a member of the government which put aside the previous decision and we said that, yes, people can be extradited to The Hague. And we never received a single threat, and I do not have a sense of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, my colleagues here advise me that what you saw on the screen that Judge Bonomy was speaking about was an interpretation error and it wasn't exactly what the witness had said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Minister, I would now like to take you to page 18 of that document. This is a story from the 30th of March of 2005, and apparently was carried on B92, but also by SENSE, Beta, and Blic. I would like, if you could read -- if you could read the first five paragraphs at the top of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because, Your Honours, the English version of this story is much reduced, and I had a sight translation by an interpreter. I think this would be of assistance. And I think the easiest way to do is ask the minister if he could read that for us and we'll get the interpretation from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean exactly? The attorney-at-law, Nebojsa Pavkovic states: We only received a message that he will prolong the weekend. I received from him only a message that he stayed longer over the weekend with his friend. This is what attorney-at-law Mr. Zivadinovic said to B92. He cannot precisely state where Pavkovic is, but he claims that he did not leave the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you continue on, please, for four more paragraphs..

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the witness please read at a slower pace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Minister, did you hear that, the interpreter is asking you to read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Zivadinovic is almost certain that his client will not appear before trial for the attempted murder of Mr. Stambolic although custody was sought for not appearing before the Tribunal. But in the message it is also mentioned that he will not appear at the trial for Stambolic and Draskovic because he believes this is an overture for him to be arrested and deported to The Hague."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: "Mr. Nebojsa Pavkovic himself stated that although seriously ill, he said that he wouldn't leave to The Hague. And in his interview to the Daily Telegraph stated that his innocence cannot be proven in The Hague and that he knows all the generals who left for the Hague and that he is not convinced that that would be a completely voluntary surrender." These are the three paragraphs you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. I would like you to read a couple more, if you would please. Could you continue on.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: "Minister of Justice, Mr. Stojkovic, said that when it comes to Mr. Pavkovic he has very little time left to surrender, and unless he does that the Republic of Serbia will implement the law."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last sentence. The witness is reading much too fast.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: He expressed his expectation that custody will be enforced for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Read a little more slowly for the benefit of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you can go back to the third line in that paragraph, I think that's where you got too fast for us. A sentence that begins with "Stojkovic."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: "Stojkovic stated for B92 that Pavkovic's refusal to appear before the special court would -- that it would present a mock trial. The police acted upon the request of the court so that they would carry out their duties. So Stojkovic, he was convinced that the police would establish Pavkovic's whereabouts and that he would be taken into custody."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you a question because I had a note from my interpretation that you're quoted as saying that in your opinion by his refusal to appear before the special court Pavkovic was "almost mocking this court." Is that an accurate translation of that term that is in quotes there? [B/C/S spoken]?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, those are my words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: May I add something to your question? I said there is little time left for him to surrender and he did surrender right after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's true. It was the preference of your government to somehow achieve voluntary surrenders rather than having to ever actually arrest any of these indictees, correct? It was certainly the preference if, indeed, not the policy.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It did bring about results. Until that time, the whereabouts of 24 people were unknown. The law prescribed two possibilities: Either a voluntary surrender or the arrest. We offered the possibility of voluntary surrendering and that they would receive the benefits offered by the government. Some of them did make use of that and the others are still on the run.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please don't get me wrong. We're grateful for what has been achieved in the presence of this accused here. But my concern is about the nature of this "voluntary surrender." You mentioned the special court there. What special court were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It is not a special court. This is what the journalists call it, but it's a separate department with the district court of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the prosecution of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, organised crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the case that this related to was a case involving the murder of Ivan Stambolic and an attempted murder of Vuk Draskovic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It pertains to those cases, but I'm not familiar with the details themselves. I know that the trials were severed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you -- what were you aware of -- you make a reference to Mr. Pavkovic's refusal to appear before that court. Do you know when that came about and how that came about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a comment for him -- of him not appearing before the court, and later an explanation was offered that it was due to illness. And I am not familiar with other comments. I wasn't a participant of the process. You know more details probably and what the reason was for not appearing. But as for the comments that are mentioned, I did give this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In -- Mr. Stojkovic, in what capacity was General Pavkovic expected to appear in the special court in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you what I read from the media because I'm not familiar with the case. It pertains to an event that took place in Budva, and under someone's order a military helicopter was provided for the transport of certain persons. This is what I know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but was he a witness? Was he an accused person? What was his capacity in the court proceeding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know his capacity. I believe he was one of the co-accused, but as to he was aiding or something else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to that, minister, if you would go to page 8 -- well, actually, I guess it's page 7 and 8 for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I want to read one sentence from paragraph -- from page 8 in the English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is from B92, the 18th of July, 2005, the bottom line on page 8 in English says: "Two other defendants in the case, former Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic and former Yugoslav army Chief of Staff, Nebojsa Pavkovic, were not sentenced because they are present in custody at The Hague Tribunal." That indicates that they are both accused in that case. Do you have any reason to dispute that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. But what is stated here is according to our law. It is the process of extraditing a person to The Hague, or whether that person is being surrendered voluntarily, then the process is set into motion awaiting a decision of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In relation to that then I have another question. If you could go to page 6 of that document. This is -- this is an article purportedly from Beta and B92 on the 9th of May, 2005. Now, I'll read from the English and ask you a question: "The council of the specialised sector of the Belgrade district court has shot down the proposal submitted by Nebojsa Pavkovic's attorney to keep his client out of confinement. "Pavkovic is wanted by the Belgrade district court in relation to the murder trial of Ivan Stambolic and the attempted murder of Vuk Draskovic, but is currently incarcerated and awaiting trial at The Hague Tribunal. "Since his attorney Ljubisa Zivadinovic's request was denied by the Belgrade district court, if Pavkovic is freed from The Hague before his trial begins and returns to Belgrade, he will be imprisoned upon his return as well." Is that -- to your knowledge, is that an accurate statement of the law in a situation as regards Mr. Pavkovic and that pending case in Belgrade? If he is released here, will he be detained there

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I am not in a position to comment that. Under our law if a person is extradited to The Hague Tribunal their process is interrupted, awaiting the ending of a procedure before The Hague Tribunal. So I don't think one can be put into custody on two different legal bases. Perhaps only after this -- these proceedings here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying then if he is released here and he goes back to Belgrade, the authorities in Belgrade will not be able to put him in custody or to hold that trial against him until this case is resolved?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because they will be awaiting the final resolution. Otherwise, what would be the point when this Tribunal does have the primacy. As I have told you, the law is clear. The previous proceedings have to be stayed until the proceedings here is finalised because this person is under the jurisdiction of this Tribunal, whether the personal surrendered voluntarily or extradited. This Tribunal has primacy. Perhaps it would be better to address this question to the Defence counsel; they are more familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The last thing I want to ask you about relates to the Prosecution's concern about the voluntariness of the surrender and future appearance for trial here. At page 5 of the document you have before you -- and, I'm sorry, it's only in English, so I'll have to read it for you. If you listen carefully and then I'll have a question for you. This purports to be from B92, Beta, and the London Sunday Times dated the 20th of June. According to the London Sunday Times: "Hague fugitive Ratko Mladic will turn himself over to The Hague Tribunal on July 11th if he gets $5 million. "The Daily writes in detail about secret discussions with Mladic Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and states that Mladic has reached an agreement to be paid $5 million to surrender on the day that the ten-year commemoration of the Srebrenica genocide. "The Sunday Times writes that sources close to those people who are negotiating with Mladic said that he wants this money for his family and body guards" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, would you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The article states: "That those behind the negotiations are Serbian oligarchs working from behind the scenes who acquired fortunes during the Milosevic regime and who wish to speed up the speed of Serbia and Montenegro process of European integration. "This circle of people used the same method, but a smaller amount of money, for getting General Nebojsa Pavkovic to surrender himself to The Hague,' the Daily writes." My question, sir, is: Do you understand the concern that if Mr. Pavkovic's surrender was as a result of receiving a large quantity of cash that we as Prosecutors would have concerns about his appearance after release because for someone who has said for a year before arriving here that he would never come, if he's released and goes back home to a suitcase full of money, he may take that money and go somewhere where we can't find him and he indeed won't return. You understand that concern, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm surprised that you take for granted what is written by B92. I have to tell you that what they wrote here is not true. Had it been true, we would have had General Mladic in our custody before the Srebrenica commemoration. This is not true. Maybe you should call the B92 people and ask them where they got this information. I truly cannot comment upon this because it is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, first I should say the story is apparently attributed to the London Sunday Times. And secondly, with regard to your statement, you said if this were true you would have Mladic here before now, you mean if he got $5 million he would have been here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. What I'm saying: Had this been true, what is stated in -- by B92, that he received five million, he probably would have been in the custody of this Tribunal before the 11th July, and that is not true. The only information that our government has is that all services are working very diligently at locating General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just one question based upon that last bit. Re-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any indication at all from any source that General Pavkovic received any money as a consideration for surrendering to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The only matter that I wish to raise is that I came here to elaborate on the guarantees. One of our guarantees is that whether the accused wants to appear here again or not, we will ensure that he does appear here. This is our guarantee. So far, we have complied with all of our obligations, and even when the accused wanted to go for treatment to Montenegro we ensured that the prior consent of this Tribunal is obtained. Therefore, we will not fail to ensure anybody's presence here before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What you're saying, then, Minister, is that it's not a matter of his will. Your government will ensure that he appears in any event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no doubt that they will come here voluntarily. However, even if they should fail to appear here voluntarily, we will ensure their presence. This is the obligation we undertake, that we will comply with all of your orders. So far, we have. There have been 12 orders so far and we have abided by all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In another proceeding in which you appeared, I recollect that the point was made that the issue of the -- of your government arresting a person for breach of a provisional release condition has not yet arisen in fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first case when you requested that a person provisionally released appear here, that was the case of Mr. Gruban, he came here voluntarily. Therefore, there was no need for us to intervene to ensure his presence here. That was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Minister, that concludes your testimony. So you may go back to the other seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, there was an issue about the health of the accused and that his ill health prevented him from surrendering earlier. What is your submission on that? What's your position on that? Because that issue hasn't been -- hasn't been raised -- hasn't been dealt with. The minister I think alluded to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the understanding that I have, and I'm quite certain it's accurate and I'll tell you in a minute that we can clear this up if you wish, the general was diagnosed with cancer. And I can tell you from my own personal experience in that regard that when you are diagnosed with cancer everything else in your life becomes relatively unimportant. And it's my understanding that it was his -- that he took the position at that time that: I've got to get this cancer operated on and under control before I surrender and go to The Hague. And he followed the advice of medical people. And as soon as the surgery was over and he had apparently recovered enough from that surgery that he felt comfortable in voluntarily surrendering he did so. I can tell you that he's had a very recent examination here regarding that cancer, and that the surgery was successful and that he has now apparently regained his health. Those of us who have gone through this know that's never a permanent thing; you have to go five years before they'll say that you're actually free of cancer. But certainly that's the situation he is in right now. Now, if Your Honours would like to hear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You did have a doctor on your witness list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We did have, and I think it was Your Honour's order that that persuaded me that that wasn't a matter of major interest. We're not asking that he be released because of his medical condition. But what I can do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But the question is how his medical condition impacted on the voluntary surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that's your question now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I can do now is I can put on the witness stand the lawyer, Zivadinovic, to testify about the medical condition because he was in contact with General Pavkovic about that throughout this whole period June of 2007 to February 2005 -- 2004 to February 2005, but I would want some assurance from the Court that he would be protected from inquiries and protected communications with General Pavkovic regarding matters other than medical. I wouldn't want the Prosecutor going into all of the conversations that he might have had with General Pavkovic about the indictment and the -- General Pavkovic's reaction to it. Because I don't want to get in a position where we are waiving the attorney/client privilege between the two of them. So that's my concern. But he could come and tell you more about the medical condition because he was present and knows about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, it's not part of your case as you make it in the motion anyway, is it? You don't say in your motion that one reason for the failure of Mr. Pavkovic to surrender earlier was his condition of health, and you haven't taken the basic step of getting a medical report to confirm or to explain it to us. So I had rather thought it wasn't part of your case at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It certainly was not part of the motion that I filed. And you're right, I have no report to support that. What I have to offer at this point is what I've told you that I have to offer, nothing more. I think the basic issue, Your Honour, is not -- is really not that. But whether he in fact voluntarily surrendered to this Tribunal, which he did. It may be that he should have surrendered earlier, but you could say that about a lot of people who have finally turned around and surrendered to this Tribunal who have now been provisionally released. Many did not surrender at all and have been provisionally released, so even though it's an issue, I don't think it is a major one. It may be to you, though, and if it is then it is a major one. But I think it's not based upon the history of provisional release here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have any further submissions, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would just like to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would like to make a brief submission to you. The Prosecutor went through all of these articles about the statements that the general had made regarding his views about surrendering to the Tribunal, and those took place over a fairly extended period of time. And as you know from the witness, there was a period of -- part of that time was a time when he was a candidate for president, so some of that speech is more political than anything. And as we know today, it really has no relationship to reality since he in fact did voluntarily surrender. Your Honours might know that we had a 65 ter conference in this case this morning, and just by way of analogy if I had announced at that 65 ter conference that I had no intention of attending this Status Conference this afternoon and then had walked in and attended it, it would have been clear that I had changed my mind. And it certainly wouldn't be evidence that I won't be here for the Status Conference on Thursday. And that's the kind of reasoning that the Prosecution is trying to use with regard to these matters. He did voluntarily surrender, and those prior statements are simply no evidence that he won't return when asked to return. The other thing that should give Your Honours a great deal of confidence is that the history of the government of Serbia in overseeing these voluntary -- these provisional releases and ensuring that people come back to the Tribunal when they are supposed to is unblemished. They have carried out, as far as I know, every condition that this Tribunal has put upon anyone who was released. There are some intensely practical reasons that I would suggest to you that favour provisional release. I know it is in the interest of Your Honours that this case proceed to trial as quickly as possible since it has been joined with cases that are very, very old. And the process of trial preparation in a case of this nature requires counsel to spend an enormous amount of time with the accused. I know Your Honours are aware of the magnitude of the evidence involved in this case. The regulations of the registrar for financial reasons will only allow one counsel to come to The Hague to visit an accused one time a month. And so that really, really impacts upon the amount of time we can spend sitting with General Pavkovic and going through the evidence that it's necessary for us to discuss with him. That preparation process would be speeded up dramatically and enhanced dramatically if he is in Belgrade where we have constant contact with him and can go through that preparation process much faster. I would suggest it could speed the preparation up as much as four months of preparation time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Am I misunderstanding the situation or are you referring exclusively to travelling costs?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you say that regulations allow for only one journey or one occasion per month when counsel can come to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If -- what's the difference if the accused is in Serbia? You would have to travel there presumably.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Our co-counsel, Your Honour, and the rest of the staff is in Belgrade, so it can all be done with e-mail and by them meeting with him, and it would be dramatically simpler. It wouldn't require me to travel there with anywhere near the frequency I might need to travel here. It still is kind of up in the air, I think, certainly from the undercurrents at least at the 65 ter conference I attended this morning, as to when it might be possible for this trial to start, but I know there is some urgency regarding that matter. The other thing that I would like to just point out to Your Honours, I'm surprised the Prosecutor raised this issue that -- contained in this article about Ratko Mladic, but on its face it's absolutely untrue. I mean, it's just one of those crazy articles that show up now and then. It says that Mladic had made a deal to get $5 million, he was going to get the money and he was going to surrender on July 11th. Well, that didn't happen, so obviously that wasn't true. And there's no evidence before you, and I tell you there can't be, as far as I know, any evidence before you that General Pavkovic received any money as a -- as a motivation to voluntarily surrender to this Tribunal. So I think any argument that that has anything to do with your decision is spurious at best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't believe that's an issue for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour. And I think -- I think you can rely on the government of Serbia to carry out what has been promised to you by the minister of justice today, and that is to get Mr. Pavkovic here, whether he wants to come here or not. And I don't think you need to worry yourselves about that. He will be here. The final thing that I want to share with you is just an understanding that I have as a result of some inquiries I made. I saw this article -- it was handed to me at the 65 ter conference this morning, these documents you have before you this afternoon, about the allegation that the general would be arrested immediately upon his return to Belgrade if he is released by this Tribunal. I immediately made inquiries into that, and I am informed that for the very reason the minister told you, because of the primacy of this Tribunal, that there is an order staying the proceedings in Belgrade until such time as the proceedings in this court are completely concluded. And that's my understanding. And if necessary, Your Honours can advise me and I can probably provide you with a copy of that order if you need it. Thank you very much for your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Anything in reply, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just briefly. I think Mr. Ackerman's analogy to having said at the 65 ter meeting this morning that he was not going to come and then two hours showing up is an imperfect analogy to the situation here. We have this accused who over a period of approximately 18 months has said repeatedly and increasingly vehemently that he was not going to come here. I can see it, he's here, he came. But I question why that happened. How did that 180-degree sea change come about? What motivated him? I can understand all kinds of things happening in a human life that causes a person to reverse their position 180 degrees. But I think a more appropriate analogy is to a biblical reference to Sol who persecuted the Christians for many months, many years and then suddenly becomes one of the most strong Christians. Well, he was struck by a bolt of lightening and went blind. We have no explanation from the Defence why this 180-degree change. And in the absence of that we have a concern about whether or not that surrender was truly voluntary and whether or not he has changed his mind about appearing and continuing to appear before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Irrespective of that, what do you say to what the minister has said, which is that the government has guaranteed and the government will see to it that he turns up?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would -- perhaps I'm a jaded cynical Prosecutor. I would have more confidence in that if there had been a better history from his government in the beginning in terms of arresting individuals. I appreciate that's difficult to overcome; that's just a matter of history, that wasn't that way. But that reluctance -- and when he was here the last time, it appeared that the -- certainly the preference, if not the policy, of that government was to do everything they possibly could to get people to appear, but they were not going to arrest them. So far they have managed to get everybody to appear, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How did Gruban appear for the 11 bis? Gruban appeared voluntarily. Yes, voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, we have not had occasion to test whether or not an arrest will actually be made, and that's our concern. Also I think it was the minister himself in relation to what Mr. Pavkovic had done by not appearing before the special division court proceedings in the case involving the murder of Stambolic and the attempted murdered of Vuk Draskovic, I think it was the minister who was quoted as saying he thought what Pavkovic had done by not appearing before that court was making a mockery of that court. Your Honour, in my jurisdiction one of the strong considerations for a court considering provisional release of someone is whether there is any prior history of failure to appear. There is one prior failure to appear by Mr. Pavkovic in that other court. Now, the reason may be he was afraid that if they showed up there he was going to be arrested and brought to The Hague. But nonetheless, that's a prior failure to appear and we think it's a factor you should consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other submissions or any other points to be raised? Mr. Caric, you're here for the government and I did not note that. So for the record, it should be noted that you're here for the government along with ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CARIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm here together with Mr. Martinovic who is a representative of the Council of Ministers. We have no matters to raise or to add to what was said by Minister Stojkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Caric.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- I'm sorry. May I simply make it clear that we are -- we are not conceding that what is reported in the press as the statements of General Pavkovic are accurate statements; in fact, it is our position that they are not. If you'll look, for instance, you will see that some of them are other people being quoted saying that General Pavkovic said that. And I think in many cases, in fact in all cases they are not completely accurate. And these are newspaper articles and we know about newspaper articles. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That concludes the hearing. We are adjourned.
